paragraphs: Training a graph neural network often involves sampling neighbors instead of processing every connection. The quality of that sampling affects the variance of the information used during training. Choosing the best sampling distribution is difficult because neighbor representations and learned aggregation weights change as training proceeds, and their current values are observed only when those neighbors are sampled.

The paper treats this decision as an adversarial bandit problem. A sampler must balance exploring neighbors to learn about their contribution to variance with exploiting its current knowledge to reduce variance immediately. This formulation accommodates changing rewards tied to node representations and learned weights, addressing a difficulty that also arises in graph attention networks.

The authors prove that their algorithm asymptotically approaches the optimal sampling variance within a factor of three. This is a qualified approximation guarantee, rather than exact optimality. Experiments across multiple datasets also support the approach's efficiency and effectiveness, connecting the theoretical sampling objective to practical graph neural network training.
neurips-2020-bandit-samplers-for-trainin.tldr: An adaptive bandit sampler handles changing graph representations and provably approaches optimal sampling variance within a factor of three asymptotically.

paragraphs: Molecule design involves finding a structure with useful properties and determining how to produce it. The paper addresses these goals together by generating synthesis instructions directly. Those instructions take the form of a directed acyclic graph, describing how simple building blocks are combined through chemical reactions into more complicated molecules.

The proposed deep generative model therefore searches over construction processes. The authors argue that this representation supplies useful inductive biases: it directs the model toward chemical possibilities accessible through the building blocks and reactions, while making the route to a proposed molecule interpretable. The synthesis graph connects a generated structure to the steps intended to create it.

The reported results show that the model represents chemical space well and produces diverse molecules. The approach also allows optimization of chemical properties within a representation that incorporates synthesizability. Its significance is that a constraint normally imposed alongside molecule search becomes part of what the model generates, so searching for desirable properties simultaneously yields a proposed synthesis route.
neurips-2020-barking-up-the-right-tree-a.tldr: Generating synthesis graphs lets a molecular design model search for desirable properties while incorporating how each molecule can be made.

paragraphs: BlockGAN learns to generate images using a scene representation that separates foreground objects from the background in three dimensions. This addresses a weakness of approaches that represent an entire scene as one object or describe its components only as image patches and flat layers. The goal is to make individual objects controllable while preserving a realistic overall image.

Its generation process follows a computer graphics pipeline. The model first creates 3D features for the background and individual foreground objects, combines them into scene features, and then renders an image. Composing objects before rendering allows it to account for occlusion and interactions in appearance, including lighting and shadows.

Training uses unlabelled single images without requiring 3D geometry, pose annotations, object masks, or multiple views of a scene. Experiments show that the explicit 3D features support separation both between objects and between properties such as pose and identity. These results support the model's ability to control an object's 3D pose and identity while maintaining image realism.
neurips-2020-blockgan-learning-3d-object.tldr: BlockGAN learns separate, controllable 3D object representations from unlabelled single images and combines them to generate realistic scenes.

paragraphs: Co-salient object detection looks for visually prominent objects that recur across a group of related images. Success requires understanding both each image and the relationships among images. CoADNet addresses this with an end-to-end network that gathers shared information from the group and then returns relevant information to each individual image.

The network first uses saliency guidance to suppress redundant background information in its features. A group attention module then aggregates semantic information across images. Next, a gated distribution module adaptively sends the resulting group representation back to individual images. This lets shared evidence influence each image according to its particular content.

A final decoder preserves group consistency while producing full-resolution maps of the co-salient objects. The design thus carries relationships across images through both feature construction and output prediction. Evaluation on four benchmark datasets reports substantial improvements over ten state-of-the-art competitors. These findings support the value of combining shared group understanding with image-specific adaptation throughout the detection process.
neurips-2020-coadnet-collaborative-aggre.tldr: CoADNet improves co-salient object detection by aggregating information across related images and adaptively distributing it back to each image.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates high-quality image generation with diffusion probabilistic models, a family of latent variable models motivated by nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Its contribution combines a training formulation with empirical image synthesis results. The central question is how to train these models so that their generated images achieve strong quality.

The best results use a weighted variational bound whose design follows a newly identified connection to denoising score matching with Langevin dynamics. This connection links the diffusion modeling approach to another framework for learning and generating from distributions. The authors also show that the models naturally support progressive lossy decompression, giving image generation an interpretation as a generalization of autoregressive decoding.

On unconditional CIFAR10 generation, the paper reports an Inception score of 9.46 and a state-of-the-art FID of 3.17. On LSUN at 256 by 256 resolution, it reports sample quality similar to ProgressiveGAN. Together, these findings establish strong image synthesis performance in the stated evaluations, while the decompression interpretation offers another way to understand the model's generation process.
neurips-2020-denoising-diffusion-probabi.tldr: Diffusion probabilistic models achieve strong image synthesis results using a training objective connected to denoising score matching.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when rewards can change adversarially across an episodic decision problem. Its setting provides full information about rewards, while the transition rules are unknown but fixed. This separates two challenges: learning how actions affect future states and adapting decisions to changing rewards.

The authors introduce two model-free policy optimization algorithms, POWER and POWER++, and analyze dynamic regret. Unlike static regret, this measure explicitly accounts for environmental non-stationarity. Their bounds span different amounts of change and achieve an adaptive form of near-optimality: when the environment changes slowly, they match the corresponding optimal or near-optimal static regret.

The analysis separates regret into exploration and adaptation components. Exploration reflects uncertainty about transitions, while adaptation reflects changing rewards. POWER++ improves the adaptation component over POWER by using prediction to respond actively to non-stationarity. This decomposition clarifies which difficulty the improvement addresses. The authors describe the work, to their knowledge, as the first dynamic regret analysis of model-free reinforcement learning in non-stationary environments.
neurips-2020-dynamic-regret-of-policy-op.tldr: POWER and POWER++ provide dynamic regret guarantees for changing rewards, with prediction improving POWER++'s adaptation component.

paragraphs: Predicting team performance and assigning credit to individuals are related problems. Cooperative game theory describes a team's performance through a characteristic function and offers contribution measures such as the Shapley Value. Applying these tools is difficult because the characteristic function usually must be learned from observations, and computing Shapley Values involves combinatorial complexity.

The paper introduces cooperative game abstractions, or CGAs, as a parametric model for learning characteristic functions. The proposed representation is interpretable and easy to learn, while allowing Shapley Values to be computed in linear time. It therefore connects estimation of team performance with an efficient way to allocate individual credit within the learned model.

The authors provide identification results, sample complexity bounds, and bounds on errors in the resulting Shapley Value estimates. These results address both learning the model and understanding the reliability of its contribution estimates. Applications cover teams of artificial reinforcement learning agents and professional sports teams, bringing the same modeling framework to computational and real-world teamwork.
neurips-2020-evaluating-and-rewarding-te.tldr: Cooperative game abstractions learn interpretable models of team performance and enable linear-time Shapley Value computation.

paragraphs: A set of vectors, such as a point cloud, contains relationships among its elements but has no meaningful input order. A model must capture those relationships while ensuring that reordering the inputs simply reorders the corresponding element features. This requirement is permutation equivariance, and it places a structural constraint on the architecture.

The paper proposes Exchangeable Neural ODE, or ExNODE, which uses ordinary differential equations to achieve this property. The authors present it as a more general formulation for modeling dependencies within sets than existing pooling and attention approaches may capture in practice. The same module can be applied to both discriminative tasks and generative tasks.

The work also extends set modeling across time through a model based on a variational autoencoder. This brings changing sets into the framework alongside individual unordered instances. Extensive experiments report effectiveness against strong baselines. The stated contribution is therefore both architectural and practical: differential equations provide a way to respect unordered structure while learning dependencies for several kinds of set modeling.
neurips-2020-exchangeable-neural-ode-for.tldr: ExNODE uses ordinary differential equations to model relationships within unordered sets while preserving permutation equivariance.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization involves understanding new combinations of familiar language components. This paper frames language understanding as predicting a partially ordered set, or poset. Such an output specifies meaningful ordering relationships without forcing every component into a single sequence. The authors argue that conventional encoder-decoder architectures inadequately reflect this semantic structure.

Their hierarchical poset decoder addresses the issue in two ways. It enforces partial permutation invariance, so rearrangements that should not change the semantics do not become a source of misleading ordering patterns. Its hierarchical mechanism also captures higher-level poset structure. Together, these choices aim to make the decoder learn semantic organization more faithfully.

The authors evaluate the decoder on Compositional Freebase Questions, a natural language question-answering dataset designed to test compositional generalization. It outperforms the existing decoders in that evaluation. The result supports the proposed connection between output representation and generalization: explicitly representing which orderings matter can help a language model handle unfamiliar combinations of semantic components.
neurips-2020-hierarchical-poset-decoding.tldr: Hierarchical poset decoding improves compositional generalization by representing semantic structure without imposing unnecessary ordering.

paragraphs: Networks formed through the actions of people or animals can reflect strategic choices made for individual or collective benefit. The paper seeks to learn those underlying choices and incentives from observed network data. Its motivation is that explaining how a network emerges can provide interpretability and flexibility beyond describing its observed structure.

The proposed framework, MINE, combines a game-theoretic account of network formation with multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning. It solves Markov-Perfect network emergence games while jointly learning agents' strategy profiles and a latent reward function. These two learned components describe how agents act during network formation and what payoffs their actions pursue.

In experiments, learned payoffs correlate highly with ground truth in a synthetic case, support analysis of observed network structure, and enable effective transfer in specific settings. The learned game also supports meaningful strategic predictions. These findings suggest that modeling network emergence as strategic interaction can serve several network analysis tasks, with the transfer result explicitly tied to the settings examined.
neurips-2020-learning-strategic-network-.tldr: MINE learns both agents' network formation strategies and their hidden payoffs through multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks offer a natural representation for physical interactions and discretized partial differential equations. However, including long-range interactions can be computationally expensive as the number of nodes grows. Omitting those interactions introduces errors that depend on discretization, making it difficult for a learned model to generalize when the mesh is refined.

Inspired by classical multipole methods, the paper proposes a multilevel graph network that captures interactions at all ranges with linear computational complexity. Its hierarchy connects the graph formulation to a matrix perspective: the construction is equivalent to recursively introducing inducing points into a kernel matrix. This links graph learning with multiresolution factorization.

Experiments show that the resulting network learns solution operators that are invariant to discretization and can be evaluated in linear time. The findings connect two goals that otherwise conflict: retaining interactions across distance and keeping computation manageable. In the reported experiments, the representation supports PDE solution prediction across discretizations rather than tying the learned operator to a particular mesh.
neurips-2020-multipole-graph-neural-oper.tldr: A multilevel graph network captures short- and long-range physical interactions in linear time and empirically learns discretization-invariant PDE solution operators.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe how a state evolves continuously over time. A basic limitation is that an ordinary differential equation's trajectory is determined by its initial condition, without an inherent mechanism for incorporating later observations. This creates a problem for time series, where new measurements should influence the evolving representation.

The paper uses controlled differential equations to introduce that influence. The resulting neural controlled differential equation model handles multivariate observations that may be incomplete and arrive at irregular times. It also permits memory-efficient adjoint-based backpropagation across observations, connecting the ability to absorb incoming data with an efficient way to train the model.

Empirical studies across several datasets report state-of-the-art performance relative to similar ODE- and recurrent-network-based models. The paper also establishes universal approximation results and shows that its formulation subsumes alternative ODE models. These theoretical findings address expressive scope, while the experiments support its practical usefulness for the irregular time-series settings evaluated.
neurips-2020-neural-controlled-different.tldr: Neural controlled differential equations incorporate incoming irregular observations into continuous-time models while supporting memory-efficient training.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation is routinely used on neural networks containing operations such as ReLU, even though the resulting functions need not be differentiable everywhere. The paper asks what mathematical correctness means in this setting. It first gives counterexamples to informal justifications, including the argument that nondifferentiable points cause no problems simply because they form a measure-zero set.

The authors study PAP functions, a class that includes nearly all of the potentially nondifferentiable functions used in deep learning considered by the paper. They introduce intensional derivatives for this class and prove that these derivatives always exist. They also establish that intensional derivatives agree with ordinary derivatives for almost all inputs.

The final link is to software: most automatic differentiation systems essentially compute, or attempt to compute, these intensional derivatives. This provides a formal basis for their use on nondifferentiable functions. The result explains correctness through a suitable derivative concept and a specified function class, while preserving the distinction between agreement almost everywhere and ordinary differentiability at every input.
neurips-2020-on-correctness-of-automatic.tldr: Intensional derivatives provide a formal correctness framework for automatic differentiation on a broad class of nondifferentiable functions.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning promises to make sequential decisions more efficiently, both in the experience needed for learning and in the computation needed for planning. The paper investigates what structure in a decision problem can support these benefits. It focuses on recurring subproblems with similar rewards and transition behavior, described as repeating subMDPs.

The authors formalize how a hierarchy can exploit this repetition and analyze a model-based algorithm using a Thompson sampling-style approach. Under the paper's assumptions, they establish statistical efficiency through a finite-time regret bound. This connects reuse of recurring structure to a quantitative guarantee about the algorithm's learning performance.

The paper separately identifies conditions under which planning with options induced by that structure is computationally efficient and near-optimal. These are distinct benefits: learning efficiently concerns acquiring useful information, while planning efficiently concerns computing decisions. The results explain how repeated subproblem structure can support both, with the guarantees depending on the stated assumptions and planning conditions.
neurips-2020-on-efficiency-in-hierarchic.tldr: The paper gives conditional learning and planning efficiency guarantees for hierarchical reinforcement learning that exploits recurring decision subproblems.

paragraphs: The paper examines a noisy linear regression setting with more freedom in the predictor than the observations can determine. In this setting, the minimum-norm predictor that fits the training data exactly is known to be consistent. The question is whether uniform convergence arguments over norm-bounded predictors can explain that successful generalization.

The authors show that uniformly controlling the difference between training error and population error cannot establish learning across the norm ball. Restricting attention to a set chosen using the algorithm and distribution still cannot establish consistency through this kind of bound. These negative results identify a mismatch between a particular proof strategy and the behavior of the interpolating predictor.

They then argue that a weaker, standard form of uniform convergence can explain consistency when applied specifically to zero-training-error predictors within the norm ball. This perspective also yields generalization bounds for interpolators with low, but not necessarily minimal, norm. The contribution thus narrows the relevant predictor class while retaining a uniform-convergence-based explanation of learning.
neurips-2020-on-uniform-convergence-and-.tldr: A weaker uniform convergence notion focused on zero-error predictors can explain low-norm interpolation where uniform error-gap bounds fail.

paragraphs: Online meta-learning uses knowledge from previous tasks to adapt quickly as new tasks arrive. A single globally shared meta-learner can be a poor fit when tasks contain different kinds of information that are difficult to share. This paper proposes organizing prior knowledge so that each task can draw on a more suitable combination.

Online structured meta-learning, or OSML, represents the meta-learner as a hierarchical graph of knowledge blocks. For a new task, it builds a pathway by selecting relevant existing blocks or exploring new ones. The model adapts through that pathway, and knowledge acquired from the task is incorporated into the selected blocks.

This structure makes transfer selective while allowing the knowledge organization to develop over time. Experiments on three datasets support the framework's effectiveness and interpretability for both heterogeneous and homogeneous task settings. The findings suggest that structured reuse can be useful even when tasks are relatively similar, while directly addressing the sharing problem that motivates the method.
neurips-2020-online-structured-meta-lear.tldr: OSML organizes transferable knowledge into a hierarchical graph and selects task-specific pathways for rapid online adaptation.

paragraphs: Solving linear systems is a basic operation throughout numerical computation, but machine learning brings particular demands involving scale, structure, randomness, and uncertainty. This paper develops probabilistic solvers that treat the computation as an inference problem. The aim includes representing uncertainty about the quantities involved as information is gathered.

The proposed class jointly infers the system matrix, its inverse, and the solution using observations of matrix-vector products. The authors derive the class from a fundamental collection of requirements that restrict which algorithms are possible. Under certain conditions, the resulting framework recovers conjugate gradients, linking the probabilistic approach to an established solver.

The paper also shows how prior spectral information can be incorporated to calibrate uncertainty. This connects knowledge about the matrix to the confidence expressed by the solver. Experiments illustrate the potential of the approach for machine learning. The contribution is a unified framework that combines linear-system computation with uncertainty inference, while retaining a conditional connection to a familiar numerical method.
neurips-2020-probabilistic-linear-solver.tldr: Probabilistic linear solvers jointly infer a matrix, its inverse, and its solution while using prior information to calibrate uncertainty.

paragraphs: A sample's profile records how frequently its symbols occur while leaving aside their identities. The paper studies profile entropy for samples from discrete distributions and shows that it connects three problems: estimating distributions, inferring symmetric properties, and compressing profiles. This places the pattern of observed frequencies at the center of the analysis.

For distribution estimation, profile entropy determines the speed of estimation relative to the best natural estimator. For symmetric properties, it characterizes inference rates relative to the best estimator over any label-invariant collection of distributions. These comparisons are central to the claims: the results describe performance against specified reference estimators and distribution collections.

Profile entropy also sets the limit for compressing profiles. The authors develop optimal block and sequential compression algorithms with near-linear running time. They further investigate the quantity's properties, give algorithms to approximate it, and determine its scale for several structured distribution families. Together, these results make profile entropy both a unifying theoretical measure and a quantity that can be studied computationally.
neurips-2020-profile-entropy-a-fundament.tldr: Profile entropy links distribution estimation, symmetric-property inference, and optimal compression of observed frequency patterns.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural network's input-output behavior does not fully explain the representation it learns internally. This paper studies that distinction in linear autoencoders. It asks whether training can recover a particular optimal representation: principal components arranged in order and aligned with the axes of the latent representation.

The authors show that appropriate regularization can produce this outcome. They analyze non-uniform L2 regularization and a deterministic version of nested dropout, establishing convergence to the desired representation for both. However, they also show that convergence is slow because of ill-conditioning, and that this problem becomes worse as the latent dimension increases.

The paper then proposes a simple change to the gradient descent update that substantially accelerates convergence in experiments. The findings separate two questions: whether the desired representation is eventually learned and how efficiently training reaches it. Regularization addresses the first, while the modified update empirically improves the second, showing that slow recovery need not be an unavoidable feature of learning principal components.
neurips-2020-regularized-linear-autoenco.tldr: Properly regularized linear autoencoders recover ordered principal components, and a modified gradient update empirically speeds their slow convergence.

paragraphs: A fixed-size determinantal point process, or k-DPP, selects a diverse subset of k items from a larger collection. Each subset's probability is proportional to a determinant computed from its kernel matrix. Existing sampling methods can require expensive preprocessing with repeated passes over the full dataset, making this appealing selection rule difficult to use at large scale.

The paper introduces alpha-DPP, which adaptively constructs a sufficiently large uniform sample and then generates the smaller requested subset from it. Crucially, the final subset follows the exact k-DPP distribution defined over the entire collection. Simple uniform subsampling followed by a k-DPP on the reduced collection does not provide that guarantee.

Empirically, alpha-DPP produces a sample after inspecting only a small fraction of the available items and achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines an exact distributional guarantee with observed computational savings. The small fraction inspected and the magnitude of acceleration are experimental findings rather than universal claims about every dataset.
neurips-2020-sampling-from-a-k-dpp-witho.tldr: Alpha-DPP preserves exact fixed-size determinantal sampling while empirically inspecting only a small fraction of the full collection.

paragraphs: Partial label learning gives each training example several candidate labels, exactly one of which is correct. Even creating these candidate sets can be expensive. This paper studies a semi-supervised setting in which examples with candidate sets are combined with completely unlabeled examples, allowing the latter to contribute to learning.

The method first uses label propagation to establish confidence values for the partially labeled examples. It then introduces a maximum-margin formulation that jointly learns a predictive model and estimates labeling confidence for unlabeled data. The objective incorporates confidence into margin maximization and preserves the manifold structure of confidence across both kinds of examples.

The resulting optimization alternates between the predictive model and labeling confidences, with each step admitting a quadratic programming solution. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the effectiveness of the approach. The contribution connects uncertainty about candidate labels with the use of additional unlabeled data, treating confidence estimation and prediction as coupled parts of the same learning process.
neurips-2020-semi-supervised-partial-lab.tldr: The method combines partial labels and unlabeled data through joint confidence estimation and confidence-rated margin maximization.

paragraphs: The paper compares Q-learning and Double Q-learning through their asymptotic mean-squared errors. Its focus is the behavior of estimation error in the long run. The analysis uses results for linear stochastic approximation based on Lyapunov equations, providing a theoretical framework for comparing the two algorithms.

The main result applies in tabular settings and with linear function approximation, provided that the optimal policy is unique and the algorithms converge. Under those assumptions, Double Q-learning has exactly the same asymptotic mean-squared error as Q-learning when two additional choices are made: its learning rate is doubled, and its reported estimate is the average of its two estimators.

This establishes a precise conditional equivalence between the methods. Both the learning-rate relationship and the averaging rule are part of the result, so the equality concerns a particular configuration of Double Q-learning. Simulations explore practical implications of the theoretical observation, connecting the asymptotic comparison to decisions about how the two estimators and learning rates are used.
neurips-2020-the-mean-squared-error-of-d.tldr: Under stated convergence and uniqueness assumptions, averaged Double Q-learning matches Q-learning's asymptotic mean-squared error when its learning rate is doubled.

paragraphs: Natural language explanations can make predictions easier to interpret and provide additional supervision, but collecting many human-written explanations is costly. This paper develops a language-understanding framework that trains with only a small set of annotated explanations. It treats explanations as latent variables intended to model the reasoning underlying a neural prediction.

Training uses a variational expectation-maximization framework. An explanation generator and a prediction module that uses explanations are optimized alternately, allowing each to improve the other. This makes explanation generation part of the prediction-learning process, with the two modules linked through a shared optimization framework.

For semi-supervised learning, the authors extend the approach with explanation-based self-training. The system alternates between assigning pseudo-labels to unlabeled examples and generating new explanations, using the two processes to improve each other iteratively. Experiments on two natural language understanding tasks report effective predictions in supervised and semi-supervised settings, alongside good generated explanations. The results support learning useful explanations and predictions with limited explanation annotation.
neurips-2020-towards-interpretable-natur.tldr: A latent-explanation framework jointly improves language predictions and generated explanations using only a small set of human-annotated explanations.

paragraphs: Functional MRI produces three-dimensional measurements that change over time. Comparing these measurements is difficult because they contain substantial noise and because brain representations vary across people. This paper proposes describing each time point through topological features, specifically high-dimensional voids, encoded in a persistence diagram.

The representation does not require voxel-by-voxel correspondence and is robust to noise. This allows comparison through topological structure rather than relying on direct alignment of individual measurement locations. The authors use sequences of persistence diagrams in two ways: clustering participants into meaningful groups and following a person's brain-state trajectory while performing a task.

The study applies both analyses to participants watching the movie Partly Cloudy. It finds significant differences between adults and children in their brain-state trajectories and overall topological activity while viewing the same movie. These observations show that the representation captures group differences and temporal structure in the studied data, supporting its usefulness for analyzing time-varying brain measurements.
neurips-2020-uncovering-the-topology-of-.tldr: Topological summaries of fMRI reveal differences in brain-state trajectories and activity between adults and children watching the same movie.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations by comparing different views of the same data, making the choice of views an important part of the learning problem. This paper studies that choice theoretically and empirically. Its central proposal is to reduce the mutual information shared by the views while retaining information relevant to the task.

The requirement to preserve task information is essential to the proposed principle. The authors develop unsupervised and semi-supervised frameworks that learn views by aiming to reduce their mutual information. They also examine data augmentation as another way to achieve this reduction, connecting a common practical technique to their information-based account.

The reported experiments show that stronger augmentation decreases mutual information and improves downstream classification accuracy. As a further result, the work reports state-of-the-art unsupervised ImageNet pretraining accuracy of 73% with a ResNet-50 and linear readout. The findings support the proposed view-selection principle in the studied settings, tying useful representation learning to reducing shared information while preserving what matters for the task.
neurips-2020-what-makes-for-good-views-f.tldr: The paper argues that effective contrastive views reduce shared information while preserving task-relevant content, supported by theory and experiments.
